questions.stem: The serpentine, rope-like parallel arrangement of the stained bacilli shown is attributed to which virulence factor?

explanation.summary: Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) causes M. tuberculosis to grow in the characteristic serpentine cords seen here and is toxic to mammalian cells while inhibiting neutrophil migration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) causes M. tuberculosis to grow in the characteristic serpentine cords seen here and is toxic to mammalian cells while inhibiting neutrophil migration.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipoteichoic acid is a gram-positive cell-envelope polymer that triggers inflammation via TLR2; it is not the mycobacterial glycolipid that produces serpentine cording.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hyaluronic acid capsule is the antiphagocytic capsule of Streptococcus pyogenes, which is nonimmunogenic because it resembles host tissue; it does not arrange bacilli in cords.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein A of S. aureus binds the Fc portion of IgG to block opsonization; it plays no role in the parallel cording of mycobacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lipoarabinomannan is a mycobacterial cell-wall glycolipid that modulates macrophage responses and is detected in urine assays, but cording is attributed to trehalose dimycolate.

questions.stem: This staining technique was used to visualize the pink bacilli shown against the blue background. What structural property of these bacteria makes this special stain necessary rather than a routine Gram stain?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A waxy, mycolic acid-rich cell wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete absence of a cell wall

explanation.summary: Mycobacteria have a lipid-rich, mycolic acid cell wall that will not take up the Gram stain, so the Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain is required; retained pink color identifies acid-fast bacilli.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacteria have a lipid-rich, mycolic acid cell wall that will not take up the Gram stain, so the Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) stain is required; retained pink color identifies acid-fast bacilli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A thick peptidoglycan layer is what makes gram-positive bacteria retain crystal violet in the routine Gram stain, so it would not require a special stain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Capsules are shown with India ink or the Quellung reaction; the capsule does not prevent Gram staining or explain retention of carbol fuchsin after acid-alcohol.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endospores resist staining and are shown with malachite green (Schaeffer-Fulton); mycobacteria do not form spores, and their acid-fastness comes from mycolic acids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Organisms with no cell wall, such as Mycoplasma, are invisible on Gram stain and do not retain acid-fast stain, unlike these pink bacilli.

questions.stem: This selective slant medium is used to culture the pathogen. Approximately how long does colony growth typically take here?

explanation.summary: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a very slow grower on Lowenstein-Jensen medium, with detection taking up to 10 days or several weeks, reflecting its long doubling time.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a very slow grower on Lowenstein-Jensen medium, with detection taking up to 10 days or several weeks, reflecting its long doubling time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth in about 24 hours is typical of fast-growing pathogens such as E. coli or staphylococci, not M. tuberculosis with its doubling time of roughly 15-20 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Two to three days fits slower routine organisms or rapidly growing mycobacteria, but M. tuberculosis takes weeks to form visible colonies on Lowenstein-Jensen medium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Visible colonies never appear within a few hours for any clinical bacterium; M. tuberculosis is one of the slowest-growing pathogens cultured.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No bacterium forms visible colonies within an hour; M. tuberculosis needs several weeks of incubation.

questions.stem: These rough, dry, buff-colored colonies with a waxy appearance are characteristic of which organism?

explanation.summary: The high mycolic acid content of the mycobacterial cell wall gives colonies their rough, waxy, buff appearance, distinct from the smooth colonies of typical bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The high mycolic acid content of the mycobacterial cell wall gives colonies their rough, waxy, buff appearance, distinct from the smooth colonies of typical bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Escherichia coli forms smooth, moist, gray colonies within a day, not dry, rough, buff, waxy colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcus aureus forms smooth, glistening, golden colonies overnight, without the rough, dry, waxy texture caused by mycolic acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Streptococcus pyogenes forms small, gray-white, beta-hemolytic colonies on blood agar, not rough, buff, waxy growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neisseria meningitidis forms smooth, moist, gray colonies on chocolate agar, unlike the dry, cauliflower-like mycobacterial colonies.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph accompanies primary tuberculosis. Which radiographic feature is most characteristic of primary TB, especially in a child?

explanation.summary: Primary TB typically shows a peripheral parenchymal (Ghon) focus with prominent hilar lymphadenopathy, unlike the apical cavitation of reactivation disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primary TB typically shows a peripheral parenchymal (Ghon) focus with prominent hilar lymphadenopathy, unlike the apical cavitation of reactivation disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bilateral upper-lobe cavitation is typical of reactivation (secondary) TB in adults, where well-oxygenated apices favor bacillary growth, not of primary infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcified pleural plaques are a marker of asbestos exposure, not a feature of primary tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diffuse fine miliary nodules indicate hematogenous dissemination; they can complicate primary TB but are not its most characteristic radiographic feature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lobar consolidation with air bronchograms is the classic appearance of typical bacterial pneumonia such as pneumococcus, not the Ghon focus with hilar adenopathy of primary TB.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph is from reactivation tuberculosis. In which lung zone do the cavitary lesions of reactivation TB characteristically appear?

explanation.summary: Reactivation TB characteristically produces cavitary disease in the well-oxygenated apices/upper lobes of the lungs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reactivation TB characteristically produces cavitary disease in the well-oxygenated apices/upper lobes of the lungs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The costophrenic angles are where pleural effusions blunt the lung base, not where reactivation TB cavitates; the bases are less oxygenated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The right middle lobe is not a preferred site of reactivation TB; disease there is classically from bronchial compression by enlarged nodes (middle lobe syndrome) rather than apical cavitation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lingula is part of the left upper lobe but lies anteriorly and inferiorly; reactivation favors the apical and posterior upper-lobe segments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lower lobes are typical for aspiration pneumonia and the primary Ghon focus, not reactivation TB, which favors the higher-oxygen apices.

questions.stem: The photograph shows administration of the tuberculin (PPD) skin test, which is read 48-72 hours later. A positive reaction represents which type of hypersensitivity?

explanation.summary: A positive PPD is a type IV reaction: memory T cells sensitized by prior infection are recruited to the injection site, release cytokines, and cause induration over 48-72 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: A positive PPD is a type IV reaction: memory T cells sensitized by prior infection are recruited to the injection site, release cytokines, and cause induration over 48-72 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A non-immune irritant reaction would appear in anyone exposed, including unsensitized people; PPD induration reflects antigen-specific memory T-cell responses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation that produces a wheal within minutes, not induration peaking at 48-72 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Type II hypersensitivity involves antibodies binding fixed cell-surface antigens, as in hemolytic anemia; it does not explain delayed induration after intradermal antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type III hypersensitivity is immune-complex deposition, like the Arthus reaction peaking at 4-12 hours, and is antibody- rather than T-cell-mediated.

questions.stem: The organized structure diagrammed here walls off the infection. Which immune process is primarily responsible for forming it?

explanation.summary: Granuloma formation is driven by cell-mediated (type IV) immunity: T cells recruit and organize macrophages (including multinucleated giant cells) around the infection, walling it off with central caseous necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granuloma formation is driven by cell-mediated (type IV) immunity: T cells recruit and organize macrophages (including multinucleated giant cells) around the infection, walling it off with central caseous necrosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type III immune-complex deposition causes vasculitis and glomerulonephritis by activating complement, not organized collections of macrophages and giant cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophil-driven abscesses are liquefied pus cavities from acute pyogenic infection, not organized epithelioid macrophage aggregates with caseous centers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type II cytotoxicity is antibody binding to cell-surface antigens with complement or ADCC-mediated destruction, not granuloma formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type I hypersensitivity is IgE-triggered mast cell degranulation producing immediate allergic responses, not the organization of macrophages around persistent antigen.

questions.stem: This illustration depicts a peripheral lung lesion together with involved hilar lymph nodes. This combined finding is a hallmark of which stage of tuberculosis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Latent infection with no visible lesion

explanation.summary: The Ghon complex (a peripheral parenchymal Ghon focus plus caseating hilar nodes) develops during primary tuberculosis infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Ghon complex (a peripheral parenchymal Ghon focus plus caseating hilar nodes) develops during primary tuberculosis infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Progressive fibrocavitary disease shows upper-lobe cavitation with fibrosis, not a small peripheral focus paired with hilar nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactivation TB arises in previously sensitized hosts and presents with apical cavitary lesions, usually without prominent hilar lymph node involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Miliary dissemination produces innumerable tiny nodules throughout the lungs from hematogenous spread, not a single peripheral lesion with hilar nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Latent infection may leave no visible lesion or only a calcified Ranke complex; the depicted active focus with involved hilar nodes is the primary Ghon complex.

questions.stem: This gross lung specimen shows innumerable small tan nodules scattered uniformly throughout the parenchyma. What mechanism produced this distribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lymphatic spread limited to one hilum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct bronchial spread from a cavity

explanation.summary: Miliary tuberculosis results when bacilli seed the bloodstream and disseminate widely, producing tiny nodules throughout the lungs and other organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Miliary tuberculosis results when bacilli seed the bloodstream and disseminate widely, producing tiny nodules throughout the lungs and other organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphatic spread confined to one hilum would enlarge hilar nodes, not scatter innumerable uniform nodules throughout both lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchial spread from a cavity produces patchy acinar or tree-in-bud nodules in dependent or adjacent segments, not a uniform millet-seed distribution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Contiguous pleural extension causes pleural thickening or effusion and subpleural disease, not nodules evenly distributed through the parenchyma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aspiration of gastric contents causes chemical pneumonitis or dependent consolidation in the lower lobes or posterior upper lobes, not innumerable uniform tan nodules.

questions.stem: This schematic shows the macrophage-driven immune response to the organism, with a cytokine activating NK cells and driving naive T cells toward a helper phenotype. What is the principal downstream consequence of this activation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Large-scale antibody production by plasma cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mast cell degranulation and histamine release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enhanced macrophage killing of intracellular bacteria

explanation.summary: IL-12 from infected macrophages activates NK cells and drives Th1 differentiation; the resulting IFN-gamma activates macrophages to kill the intracellular mycobacteria, the core of cell-mediated defense.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-12 from infected macrophages activates NK cells and drives Th1 differentiation; the resulting IFN-gamma activates macrophages to kill the intracellular mycobacteria, the core of cell-mediated defense.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Large-scale antibody production by plasma cells is driven by Th2 and T follicular helper help, and antibodies are ineffective against bacilli hidden inside macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mast cell degranulation and histamine release reflect IgE-mediated type I responses, not IL-12-driven Th1 immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophil recruitment against helminths is a Th2 response mediated by IL-5, the opposite arm from the IL-12/IFN-gamma Th1 axis shown.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Complement-mediated lysis requires membrane attack complex insertion into exposed outer membranes, and mycobacteria within macrophages are not cleared this way.

questions.stem: This overview schematic contrasts primary and secondary tuberculosis outcomes. In an immunocompetent person, what is the most common outcome after primary infection?

explanation.summary: In roughly 90% of immunocompetent patients, primary infection is contained within a latent granuloma, and the patient remains asymptomatic for years.
explanation.whyCorrect: In roughly 90% of immunocompetent patients, primary infection is contained within a latent granuloma, and the patient remains asymptomatic for years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Miliary dissemination is an uncommon outcome, seen mainly in infants, the elderly, or immunocompromised hosts, not the usual result in immunocompetent people.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tuberculous meningitis is a rare, severe complication of hematogenous spread, mostly in young children or immunocompromised patients, not the typical outcome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cavitary disease is the hallmark of reactivation TB years later, not of primary infection in an immunocompetent host.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune control takes weeks to develop, and viable bacilli persist in granulomas for years, so sterilization within 24 hours does not occur.

questions.stem: This three-panel schematic illustrates the reaction underlying a positive PPD test over 24-72 hours. Which cells are the principal mediators of the visible lesion that develops?

explanation.summary: The delayed-type (type IV) reaction is driven by sensitized T cells that recognize injected antigen and recruit macrophages, producing the palpable induration.
explanation.whyCorrect: The delayed-type (type IV) reaction is driven by sensitized T cells that recognize injected antigen and recruit macrophages, producing the palpable induration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement proteins mediate immune-complex and antibody-triggered injury, not the T-cell- and macrophage-driven induration of a delayed-type reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgE-armed mast cells cause immediate wheal-and-flare reactions within minutes, not induration that develops over 48-72 hours.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils forming pus characterize acute pyogenic infection or Arthus reactions; the PPD lesion is a lymphocyte and macrophage infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Circulating antibodies mediate type I-III reactions; a positive PPD can occur without antibody and depends on sensitized T cells.

questions.stem: This transmission electron micrograph shows a host cell containing a single large membrane-bound structure packed with small particles. What is this structure?

explanation.summary: Chlamydia species replicate inside a membrane-bound endosome (inclusion) within the host-cell cytoplasm, which enlarges as the bacteria multiply and can eventually dominate the cell volume.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia species replicate inside a membrane-bound endosome (inclusion) within the host-cell cytoplasm, which enlarges as the bacteria multiply and can eventually dominate the cell volume.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of rabies virus in neurons, seen as dense masses rather than a membrane-bound vacuole packed with bacterial particles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mycoplasma usually attaches to the outer surface of host cells rather than growing in a single large cytoplasmic membrane-bound vacuole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A mitotic nucleus would show condensed chromosomes without an intact surrounding membrane, not a vacuole full of uniform small particles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A phagolysosome contains heterogeneous degraded material, whereas the chlamydial inclusion avoids lysosomal fusion and fills with uniform elementary and reticulate bodies.

questions.stem: This colorized micrograph captures the final step of an intracellular bacterial cycle, with numerous small particles bursting from the host cell. What event is occurring?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Biofilm formation on the cell surface

explanation.summary: At the end of the chlamydial cycle, reticulate bodies convert back to elementary bodies and the infected cell lyses, releasing infectious elementary bodies that go on to infect neighboring cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the end of the chlamydial cycle, reticulate bodies convert back to elementary bodies and the infected cell lyses, releasing infectious elementary bodies that go on to infect neighboring cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sporulation forms a single resistant endospore inside a Bacillus or Clostridium cell; it is not a release of many particles from a lysing host cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enveloped virions bud individually through the host membrane without lysing the cell, whereas Chlamydia exits by bursting the cell or by extrusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phagocytosis is the uptake of particles into a cell, the reverse of particles bursting out at the end of an intracellular cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A biofilm is an extracellular matrix-encased community on a surface, not release of infectious particles from a ruptured host cell.

questions.stem: This electron micrograph shows the labeled bacterium residing within a human phagocyte. Which mechanism allows the organism to survive inside this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks the oxidative burst with catalase

choices.label: B
choices.text: It prevents fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It neutralizes phagosomal acid with urease

choices.label: D
choices.text: It escapes into the cytosol using a pore-forming toxin

choices.label: E
choices.text: It forms a thick antiphagocytic capsule

explanation.summary: Legionella pneumophila is a facultative intracellular pathogen taken up by macrophages via coiling phagocytosis; it then inhibits phagosome-lysosome fusion, allowing it to persist and replicate inside the phagocyte.
explanation.whyCorrect: Legionella pneumophila is a facultative intracellular pathogen taken up by macrophages via coiling phagocytosis; it then inhibits phagosome-lysosome fusion, allowing it to persist and replicate inside the phagocyte.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase protects organisms such as S. aureus and Nocardia from peroxide, but Legionella's key survival strategy is blocking phagosome-lysosome fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Urease-mediated acid neutralization is how Helicobacter pylori survives gastric acid, not how Legionella persists within macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Escaping into the cytosol with a pore-forming toxin is the strategy of Listeria (listeriolysin O); Legionella stays in a modified vacuole.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An antiphagocytic capsule prevents uptake in the first place, but the bacterium shown is already inside the phagocyte and survives there.

questions.stem: A young adult with a two-week history of low-grade fever and a persistent dry cough has this chest radiograph, whose lung findings look worse than the mild clinical symptoms. Which radiographic pattern is most characteristic of the responsible organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Large pleural effusion with a meniscus sign

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical ('walking') pneumonia in which lung involvement on imaging is characteristically streaky/patchy interstitial infiltrates that appear worse than the patient's mild symptoms, rather than the dense lobar consolidation of typical bacterial pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical ('walking') pneumonia in which lung involvement on imaging is characteristically streaky/patchy interstitial infiltrates that appear worse than the patient's mild symptoms, rather than the dense lobar consolidation of typical bacterial pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A large pleural effusion with a meniscus sign suggests parapneumonic effusion or empyema, which are uncommon with Mycoplasma's mild walking pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dense lobar consolidation is typical pneumococcal pneumonia with abrupt high fever and productive cough, not the mild subacute dry-cough illness described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An upper-lobe cavitary lesion suggests reactivation TB, anaerobic abscess, or S. aureus, not Mycoplasma infection in a young adult.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is classic for sarcoidosis or some fungal infections, not Mycoplasma pneumonia.

questions.stem: This electron micrograph shows a tiny bacterium that is markedly variable in shape (pleomorphic) with no definitive form. Which structural feature best explains this appearance and its resistance to beta-lactams?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall entirely, so it has no fixed shape and appears pleomorphic; the absence of peptidoglycan also makes cell-wall-active antibiotics (beta-lactams) ineffective.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycoplasma pneumoniae lacks a cell wall entirely, so it has no fixed shape and appears pleomorphic; the absence of peptidoglycan also makes cell-wall-active antibiotics (beta-lactams) ineffective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A waxy mycolic-acid coat belongs to mycobacteria, which keep a rod shape and a peptidoglycan layer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A polysaccharide capsule is an outer coat that resists phagocytosis but gives no structural rigidity, and encapsulated organisms with cell walls remain beta-lactam targets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An LPS-containing outer membrane belongs to gram-negative bacteria, which still have peptidoglycan and fixed shapes, and many are beta-lactam susceptible.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A thick peptidoglycan layer is a gram-positive feature that confers a fixed shape and is the target of beta-lactams, the opposite of pleomorphism and resistance.

questions.stem: These colonies with a dense center and translucent periphery ('fried-egg' appearance) grew only after the culture medium was supplemented with a specific lipid. Which growth requirement identifies this organism?

explanation.summary: Mycoplasma is unique among bacteria in incorporating sterols such as cholesterol into its membrane and therefore requires sterol-supplemented media to grow; the resulting colonies show the classic fried-egg morphology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycoplasma is unique among bacteria in incorporating sterols such as cholesterol into its membrane and therefore requires sterol-supplemented media to grow; the resulting colonies show the classic fried-egg morphology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated CO2 enhances growth of capnophiles such as Neisseria and Haemophilus, but it is not the lipid supplement needed for fried-egg Mycoplasma colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemin (factor X) is required by Haemophilus, which forms small gray colonies on chocolate agar, not fried-egg colonies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cysteine and iron are required by Legionella on BCYE agar, not by Mycoplasma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NAD (factor V) is a Haemophilus requirement, not a lipid, and does not explain fried-egg colonies.

questions.stem: This rapid lateral-flow urine antigen assay is a common field method for diagnosing Legionnaires' disease. What is its principal diagnostic limitation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot detect any serogroup of L. pneumophila

choices.label: C
choices.text: It turns positive only after three weeks of illness

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires a fresh sputum sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: It detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1

explanation.summary: The urine antigen test detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1; because that serogroup causes about 90% of cases it remains very useful, but PCR or culture is needed to catch the other serogroups.
explanation.whyCorrect: The urine antigen test detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1; because that serogroup causes about 90% of cases it remains very useful, but PCR or culture is needed to catch the other serogroups.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The test does detect L. pneumophila, specifically serogroup 1, which causes most cases; it is not blind to all serogroups.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cross-reactivity with pneumococcus is not its key limitation; a separate pneumococcal urine antigen test exists for S. pneumoniae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Legionella urinary antigen often becomes positive within the first days of illness and can persist for weeks, so it is not delayed to three weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The assay uses urine, not sputum, which is an advantage because many patients with Legionnaires' disease have little sputum.

questions.stem: This fastidious organism grew as the dark colonies shown only on buffered charcoal yeast extract agar and stains poorly on Gram stain. Which two supplements does it specifically require for growth?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hemin and NAD (factors X and V)

explanation.summary: Legionella pneumophila requires cysteine and iron, supplied by buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar; because it stains poorly with Gram stain, a silver stain is used to visualize it in tissue or sputum.
explanation.whyCorrect: Legionella pneumophila requires cysteine and iron, supplied by buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar; because it stains poorly with Gram stain, a silver stain is used to visualize it in tissue or sputum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholesterol and sterols are required by Mycoplasma, which lacks a cell wall, not by Legionella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mannitol and high salt make up mannitol salt agar, which selects for staphylococci, not BCYE agar.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cystine-tellurite medium (Tinsdale agar) is used to grow Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which forms black colonies with brown halos.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemin and NAD (factors X and V) are required by Haemophilus influenzae, which grows on chocolate agar, not BCYE.

questions.stem: This schematic depicts the biphasic developmental cycle of the organism. Why can this bacterium replicate only inside host cells?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It needs host cholesterol to build its cell wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is killed by exposure to extracellular oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It cannot replicate its own DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: It lacks ribosomes for protein synthesis

explanation.summary: Chlamydia are obligate intracellular bacteria historically mistaken for viruses because they cannot generate sufficient ATP and rely on host-cell energy; the cycle alternates infectious elementary bodies with replicating reticulate bodies inside the inclusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chlamydia are obligate intracellular bacteria historically mistaken for viruses because they cannot generate sufficient ATP and rely on host-cell energy; the cycle alternates infectious elementary bodies with replicating reticulate bodies inside the inclusion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chlamydiae do not need host cholesterol to build a cell wall; sterol dependence is a feature of Mycoplasma membranes, and chlamydial obligate parasitism reflects energy dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elementary bodies survive extracellular conditions to spread infection; Chlamydia is not killed by oxygen, and its intracellular dependence relates to ATP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chlamydiae have their own DNA polymerase and replicate their genomes by binary fission as reticulate bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chlamydiae have their own 70S ribosomes and synthesize proteins, which is why macrolides and tetracyclines are effective.

questions.stem: This photographic plate compares the four labeled feeding stages of the tick vector shown. Which of these stages is the usual culprit in transmitting Lyme disease?

explanation.summary: The immature nymph is small and easily overlooked, so it typically remains attached long enough (36-48 h) to transmit Borrelia burgdorferi. The larger adult forms are usually noticed and removed before transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: The immature nymph is small and easily overlooked, so it typically remains attached long enough (36-48 h) to transmit Borrelia burgdorferi. The larger adult forms are usually noticed and removed before transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult females can transmit Borrelia, but their larger size means they are usually noticed and removed before the 36-48 hours of attachment needed for transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adult males feed briefly or not at all and rarely stay attached long enough to transmit Lyme disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Larvae hatch uninfected because Borrelia is not passed transovarially; they acquire it from their first blood meal on infected mice.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eggs do not feed and do not carry Borrelia, so an egg mass cannot transmit Lyme disease.

questions.stem: This expanding, target-like skin lesion with central clearing is considered pathognomonic for the early localized stage of which infection?

explanation.summary: Erythema migrans, the bull's-eye rash, appears in 70-80% of Lyme disease patients during stage 1 and is the hallmark early sign of Borrelia burgdorferi infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythema migrans, the bull's-eye rash, appears in 70-80% of Lyme disease patients during stage 1 and is the hallmark early sign of Borrelia burgdorferi infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tinea corporis forms annular plaques with central clearing, but the border is scaly and raised, and it spreads slowly over weeks without systemic features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bacterial cellulitis is a warm, tender, poorly demarcated spreading erythema without central clearing or a target pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ehrlichiosis typically causes fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated transaminases; rash is uncommon and is not a target lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rocky Mountain spotted fever causes a petechial rash that begins on wrists and ankles and spreads centripetally, not a single expanding bull's-eye lesion.

questions.stem: This infographic illustrates blistering, disseminated, bull's-eye, and blue-red variants of a single rash. All of these presentations are caused by which organism?

explanation.summary: The figure shows the many morphologies the Lyme disease rash can take. All are manifestations of infection by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi; the rash may also be absent entirely.
explanation.whyCorrect: The figure shows the many morphologies the Lyme disease rash can take. All are manifestations of infection by the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi; the rash may also be absent entirely.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Rickettsia rickettsii causes a centripetal maculopapular to petechial rash from vasculitis, not the expanding annular erythema migrans variants shown.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Treponema pallidum causes a painless chancre and then a diffuse copper-colored rash including palms and soles in secondary syphilis, not erythema migrans.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ehrlichia chaffeensis infects monocytes and causes a febrile illness with cytopenias; rash is uncommon and not bull's-eye.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leptospira interrogans causes fever, conjunctival suffusion, and in severe cases Weil disease with jaundice and renal failure, not erythema migrans variants.

questions.stem: This maculopapular rash, which begins on the wrists, ankles, palms, and soles before spreading toward the trunk, arises because the causative bacterium preferentially infects which cell type?

explanation.summary: Rickettsia rickettsii invades endothelial cells lining blood vessels, producing a vasculitis that manifests as the centripetal maculopapular (and later petechial) rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rickettsia rickettsii invades endothelial cells lining blood vessels, producing a vasculitis that manifests as the centripetal maculopapular (and later petechial) rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mononuclear phagocytes are infected by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which forms morulae and rarely causes rash; R. rickettsii targets endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Red blood cells are infected by Babesia and Plasmodium, causing hemolysis rather than a vasculitic rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocytes are the target of hepatitis viruses and of the liver stage of malaria, not of rickettsiae causing a vasculitic rash.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peripheral neurons are invaded by viruses such as rabies, HSV, and VZV; rickettsial rash arises from endothelial infection and leaky vessels.
